paper.source: DSSSB PGT Mathematics (post code 825/24), computer-based test of 13 April 2026, shift 1: the mathematics section (questions 101 to 280) of the board's response sheet as re-shared after the exam, with the board's draft-stage answer key
paper.note: The mathematics section of the paper; the whole paper had 300 questions in 180 minutes.

en.q: In how many ways can a school schedule 5 exams so that Math and Science subjects are never together?
en.explanation:
All orders of the 5 exams: $5! = 120$.
Orders with Math and Science together: glue them into one block, $4! \times 2! = 48$.
Never together: $120 - 48 = 72$.
notes: $4! = 24$ only arranges four units and forgets the rest of the count.
$5! = 120$ counts every order, including those with the two exams side by side.
Double the right answer: an extra factor 2 slipped in.
facts: Never together = total − together, where 'together' = (units with the block) × (orders inside the block).

en.q: Let $A = \{1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 9, 11\}$ and $B = \{x \in \mathbb{N} :$ $x$ is an odd prime number less than $10\}$ be two sets. Then which one of the following is 'NOT' correct? ($\mathbb{N}$: natural number set)
options: The power set of $A \cap B$ contains 4 elements
en.explanation:
$B = \{3, 5, 7\}$ and $A \cap B = \{3, 7\}$, which is not $B$ (5 is missing): (a) is the false one.
Check the rest: $A \cap B$ has 2 elements, so its power set has $2^2 = 4$; $A \cup (A \cap B) = A$ always; $A - B$ removes 3 and 7, leaving $\{1, 2, 6, 9, 11\}$.
notes: False: $5 \in B$ but $5 \notin A$, so $A \cap B \ne B$.
facts: Absorption: $A \cup (A \cap B) = A$; a set with $n$ elements has $2^n$ subsets.

en.q: Let $P = \{a, b, c\}$, $Q = \{1, 2, 3\}$ and $R = \{a, c, 5, 6\}$ be three sets. The total number of possible relations that can be defined from a set $Q$ to the set $B = (P \cap R)$ is equal to
en.explanation:
$B = P \cap R = \{a, c\}$, so $Q \times B$ has $3 \times 2 = 6$ ordered pairs.
A relation from $Q$ to $B$ is any subset of $Q \times B$: $2^6 = 64$.
notes: 6 is the number of ordered pairs, not of relations.
$2 \times 6$: multiplying instead of raising 2 to the power 6.
facts: Number of relations from an $m$-set to an $n$-set $= 2^{mn}$.

en.q: Suppose $g$ is a function defined by $g(a) = \dfrac{1 - a}{1 + a}$, $a \ne -1$. Find $g^{-1}(a)$.
en.explanation:
Put $y = \frac{1 - a}{1 + a}$. Then $y + ya = 1 - a$, so $a(1 + y) = 1 - y$ and $a = \frac{1 - y}{1 + y}$.
So $g^{-1}(a) = \frac{1 - a}{1 + a} = g(a)$: $g$ is its own inverse.
notes: The reciprocal $\frac{1 + a}{1 - a}$ is not the inverse function.
facts: $x \mapsto \frac{1 - x}{1 + x}$ is self-inverse: applying it twice gives $x$ back.

en.q: Let $R$ be a relation on set $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}$ defined by $R = \{(1, 1),\allowbreak (2, 2),\allowbreak (3, 3),\allowbreak (4, 4),\allowbreak (1, 3),\allowbreak (3, 1),\allowbreak (2, 4),\allowbreak (4, 2)\}$. Which property does $R$ satisfy?
options: Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
en.explanation:
Reflexive: $(1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4)$ are all in $R$.
Symmetric: $(1,3), (3,1)$ and $(2,4), (4,2)$ come in pairs.
Transitive: every chain stays inside $\{1, 3\}$ or inside $\{2, 4\}$, e.g. $(1,3), (3,1) \Rightarrow (1,1) \in R$. So $R$ is an equivalence relation, with classes $\{1, 3\}$ and $\{2, 4\}$.
notes: It is also reflexive and transitive.
It is transitive too: no chain leaves its class.
It is also symmetric and transitive.
facts: A relation that is all pairs within the blocks of a partition is an equivalence relation.

en.q: In the proof of Mathematical Induction of $3^n > n^3$ for $n \ge 4$, which of the following is the conclusion of inductive step?
en.explanation:
Inductive step: assume $P(k)$: $3^k > k^3$ for some $k \ge 4$, and prove $P(k + 1)$.
The conclusion to be reached is $P(k + 1)$: $3^{k+1} > (k + 1)^3$.
notes: This is the induction hypothesis $P(k)$, not the conclusion.
Weaker than $P(k+1)$: the right side must become $(k+1)^3$.
facts: Induction step: assume $P(k)$, conclude $P(k + 1)$.

en.q: For any natural number $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $9^n - 4^n$ is divisible by
en.explanation:
$a^n - b^n$ is always divisible by $a - b$, here $9 - 4 = 5$.
Check: $n = 1$ gives 5; $n = 2$ gives $81 - 16 = 65 = 5 \times 13$.
notes: $9^n - 4^n$ is odd minus even, so it is odd.
facts: $a^n - b^n$ is divisible by $a - b$ for every $n$, and by $a + b$ when $n$ is even.

en.q: Which of the following relations from set $A = \{1, 2, 3\}$ to set $B = \{4, 5, 6\}$ is a function?
en.explanation:
A function from $A$ gives each of 1, 2, 3 exactly one image.
(a): 3 has two images. (c): 1 has two images and 3 has none. (d): 2 has two images and 3 has none. Only (b) works.
notes: Each element of $A$ has exactly one image.
facts: Function: every element of the domain has exactly one image.

en.q: If $A = \{2,3,7\}$ and $B = \{5,9\}$ then which of the following is the function from $A$ to $B$?
en.explanation: Each of 2, 3, 7 must appear exactly once as a first entry. Only (b) does: $2 \mapsto 5$, $3 \mapsto 5$, $7 \mapsto 9$ (two elements may share an image).
notes: 2 and 7 have two images each; 3 has none.
This is all of $A \times B$: every element has two images.
facts: Many-one is allowed in a function; one-many is not.

en.q: Which of the following sets is non empty set?
en.explanation:
$x^2 = 0$ has the real solution $x = 0$, so the set is $\{0\}$: not empty.
$|x| < 0$ is impossible; $x^2 = -6$ has no real root; $x^2 = 2$ gives $\pm\sqrt2$, which are not natural numbers.
notes: A square is never negative: empty.
facts: $\{0\}$ is not the empty set: it has one element.

en.q: Which of the following best defines a set?
options: A collection of random objects with no definite rule.
A well-defined collection of distinct objects.
A list of objects that can be repeated any number of times.
A group of similar objects arranged in a sequence.
en.explanation: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects: for any object we can decide whether it belongs, and repeating an element does not change the set.
notes: Without a definite rule membership cannot be decided.
Repetition is ignored in a set: $\{1, 1, 2\} = \{1, 2\}$.
Order does not matter in a set; that describes a sequence.
facts: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects; order and repetition do not matter.

en.q: Principle of Mathematical Induction is a method used to prove statements:
en.explanation: Induction proves $P(1)$ and $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k + 1)$; together these reach every natural number, because $\mathbb{N}$ is built by repeatedly adding 1 (Peano's axiom of induction).
notes: The reals cannot be reached by steps of 1.
Plain induction does not reach the negative integers.
The rationals cannot be listed by steps of 1.
facts: Induction works on $\mathbb{N}$ (or on any set listed as $n_0, n_0 + 1, n_0 + 2, \dots$).

en.q: One of the values of $x$ not in the domain of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{2x - 1}{x^2 - 4}$ is ____
en.explanation: $f$ is undefined where the denominator is zero: $x^2 - 4 = 0$, $x = \pm 2$. So $x = -2$ is not in the domain.
notes: This only makes the numerator zero, so $f(\frac12) = 0$ is defined.
facts: Domain of a rational function: all reals except the zeros of the denominator.

en.q: If $A$ and $B$ are two sets given as $A = \{1,5,3,8,9\}$ and $B = \{2,4,5,9\}$ then $A \cap B$ and $A \cup B$ are respectively given as
en.explanation:
Common elements: 5 and 9, so $A \cap B = \{5, 9\}$.
All elements: $A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 9\}$. Check: $n(A \cup B) = 5 + 4 - 2 = 7$.
notes: Misses 9 in the intersection and 8 in the union.
facts: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$ is a quick check.

facts: ${}^nP_r = r! \times {}^nC_r$, so $\frac{{}^nP_r}{{}^nC_r} = r!$.

en.q: The expression $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k + 1)}$ is equal to:
en.explanation:
$\frac{1}{k(k + 1)} = \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k + 1}$, so the sum telescopes:
$\left(1 - \frac12\right) + \left(\frac12 - \frac13\right) + \dots + \left(\frac1n - \frac{1}{n+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n + 1} = \frac{n}{n + 1}$.
notes: Greater than 1; the sum is always less than 1.
This is the last term left over, not the sum.
For $n = 1$ this gives 1, but the sum is $\frac12$.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $\frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \frac1k - \frac{1}{k+1}$: the sum to $n$ terms is $\frac{n}{n+1}$.

en.q: Find the number of permutations of the letters of the word VARANASI.
en.explanation:
VARANASI has 8 letters: A three times, and V, R, N, S, I once each.
Number of arrangements $= \frac{8!}{3!} = \frac{40320}{6} = 6720$.
notes: More than $8! = 40320$, the count even with all letters distinct.
facts: Arrangements of $n$ letters with one letter repeated $p$ times: $\frac{n!}{p!}$.

en.q: Using Pascal's Triangle, the coefficients for the expansion of $(a + b)^8$ are given as
en.explanation:
Row 8 of Pascal's triangle is ${}^8C_0, \dots, {}^8C_8$: 1, 8, 28, 56, 70, 56, 28, 8, 1.
Checks: 9 numbers, symmetric, total $2^8 = 256$.
facts: Row $n$ of Pascal's triangle has $n + 1$ entries, is symmetric and adds up to $2^n$.

en.q: If $a, b, c$ are in arithmetic progression (AP) and $a \ne c$, then the value of $\dfrac{b - a}{c - b}$ is equal to
en.explanation: In an AP, $b - a = c - b = d$, and $d \ne 0$ because $a \ne c$. So the ratio is $\frac{d}{d} = 1$.
notes: Would need $b = a$, i.e. $d = 0$ and $a = c$, which is excluded.
Would need $b - a = b - c$, i.e. $a = c$, which is excluded.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $a, b, c$ in AP $\iff 2b = a + c \iff b - a = c - b$.

en.q: Value of ${}^nC_r + {}^nC_{r-1}$:
en.explanation:
Pascal's rule: ${}^nC_r + {}^nC_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_r$ (to choose $r$ of $n + 1$ objects, a fixed object is either left out, ${}^nC_r$ ways, or taken, ${}^nC_{r-1}$ ways).
Check $n = 3$, $r = 1$: $3 + 1 = 4 = {}^4C_1$.
facts: ${}^nC_r + {}^nC_{r-1} = {}^{n+1}C_r$: the rule that builds Pascal's triangle.

en.q: The middle term in the binomial expansion of $\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)^{10}$ is:
en.explanation: There are 11 terms, so the middle one is $T_6 = \binom{10}{5} x^5 \left(\frac1x\right)^5 = \binom{10}{5} x^0 = 252$.
notes: The powers of $x$ in $T_6$ cancel exactly.
facts: In $\left(x + \frac1x\right)^{2m}$ the middle term $\binom{2m}{m}$ is independent of $x$.

en.q: Which of the following is correct for any three non-zero numbers? "$a, b, c$" are in Geometric progression.
en.explanation:
In a GP, $\frac{b}{a} = \frac{c}{b} = r$, so $b^2 = ac$: the middle term is the geometric mean of its neighbours.
Check 2, 6, 18: $6^2 = 36 = 2 \times 18$.
notes: Middle term squared = product of the outer terms.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $a, b, c$ in GP $\iff b^2 = ac$.

en.explanation:
${}^nC_x = {}^nC_y$ with $x \ne y$ means $x + y = n$, so $n = 5 + 2 = 7$.
Then ${}^7C_7 = 1$.
facts: ${}^nC_x = {}^nC_y \Rightarrow x = y$ or $x + y = n$.

en.q: If 3 geometric means are inserted between 1 and 81, what is the 2nd geometric mean?
en.explanation:
1, $G_1$, $G_2$, $G_3$, 81 is a GP of 5 terms: $r^4 = 81$, $r = 3$.
The means are 3, 9, 27; the 2nd is 9. (It is also $\sqrt{1 \times 81}$, the middle term.)
notes: This is the last term, not a mean.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: With $n$ GMs between $a$ and $b$: $r = (b/a)^{1/(n+1)}$.

en.q: If two geometric means $G_1$ and $G_2$ are inserted between 3 and 75, then the largest value of $G_1$ and $G_2$ is
en.explanation:
3, $G_1$, $G_2$, 75 is a GP: $3r^3 = 75$, $r^3 = 25$, $r = 25^{1/3}$.
$G_1 = 3 \cdot 25^{1/3} \approx 8.77$ and $G_2 = 3r^2 = 3 \cdot 25^{2/3} \approx 25.65$, the larger.
Note: $3 \cdot 25^{2/3} = 3 \cdot 5^{4/3} = 15 \cdot 5^{1/3}$. The paper prints (b) with a full stop, $15.5^{1/3}$ (a decimal, about 2.49); if that stop were meant as multiplication, (b) would be the same number as (a).
notes: Read as a decimal, $15.5^{1/3} \approx 2.49$, less than the first term 3.
Read as a decimal, $25.3^{2/3} \approx 8.6$: about $G_1$, not $G_2$.
Read as a decimal, $3.5^{2/3} \approx 2.3$, less than the first term.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: Two GMs between $a$ and $b$ are $ar$ and $ar^2$, with $r = (b/a)^{1/3}$.

en.q: What is the value of $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{x}$?
en.explanation: $\frac{e^{2x} - 1}{x} = 2 \cdot \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{2x} \to 2 \times 1 = 2$, using $\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{e^t - 1}{t} = 1$.
facts: $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{e^{kx} - 1}{x} = k$.

en.q: The binomial theorem is crucial for solving what type of problems?
options: Problems related to combinatorics and algebraic expansions
Problems involving calculus and differential equations
en.explanation: The binomial theorem expands $(a + b)^n = \sum {}^nC_r a^{n-r} b^r$; its coefficients ${}^nC_r$ are the counting numbers of combinatorics. It is the tool for expansions, coefficients and approximations.
facts: Binomial coefficients ${}^nC_r$ link algebraic expansion with counting.

en.q: The middle term in $(y + x)^{10}$ is:
en.explanation: $n = 10$ is even, so there are 11 terms and a single middle term, $T_{\frac{n}{2} + 1} = T_6$.
notes: $T_5$ has 4 terms before it and 6 after.
For odd $n$ there are two middle terms, but they are not added; here $n$ is even.
The 10th of 11 terms is near the end.
facts: $(a+b)^n$, $n$ even: one middle term $T_{n/2+1}$; $n$ odd: two middle terms.

en.q: If $7^{\text{th}}$ term and $12^{\text{th}}$ term of an arithmetic progression be 34 and 59, then its $15^{\text{th}}$ term is:

en.q: In the binomial expansion of $(1 + ax)^n$, the first three terms are $1, 10x, 40x^2$. Find the value of $n$
en.explanation:
$na = 10$ and $\frac{n(n - 1)}{2} a^2 = 40$.
Divide the second by the square of the first: $\frac{n - 1}{2n} = \frac{40}{100}$, so $5n - 5 = 4n$ and $n = 5$ (with $a = 2$).
notes: Then $a = \frac54$ and the $x^2$ coefficient is 43.75, not 40.
facts: $(1 + ax)^n = 1 + nax + \frac{n(n-1)}{2}a^2x^2 + \dots$

en.q: Let $a$ and $b$ respectively denote the values of the term independent of $x$ and the coefficient of $x^2$ in the expansion of $\left(2x - \frac{3}{x}\right)^4$. Then the value of $a + b$ is

en.q: For every natural number $n \ge 2$, if $P(n)$: $\sqrt{n}$ and $Q(n)$: $\frac{1}{\sqrt1} + \frac{1}{\sqrt2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt3} + \dots + \frac{1}{\sqrt n}$, then the relation between $P(n)$ and $Q(n)$ is _____.
en.explanation:
For $k \le n$, $\frac{1}{\sqrt k} \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt n}$, with strict inequality for $k < n$. So for $n \ge 2$:
$Q(n) > n \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt n} = \sqrt n = P(n)$.
Check $n = 2$: $1 + 0.707 = 1.707 > 1.414$.
notes: Each of the $n$ terms is at least $\frac{1}{\sqrt n}$.
facts: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{\sqrt k} > \sqrt n$ for $n \ge 2$.

en.q: The sum of the four AM between 3 and 23 is:
en.explanation:
The sum of $n$ AMs between $a$ and $b$ is $n \cdot \frac{a + b}{2} = 4 \times 13 = 52$.
(The AMs are 7, 11, 15, 19.)
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: Sum of $n$ arithmetic means between $a$ and $b$ $= n \cdot \frac{a+b}{2}$.

en.q: The sum of cubes of the first 10 natural numbers is:
en.explanation:
$\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^3 = \left(\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\right)^2$. For $n = 10$: $55^2 = 3025$.
(The paper prints options (c) and (d) as 553 and 552: the exponents were lost, as in other options of this paper.)
notes: 55 is the sum of the first 10 numbers, not of their cubes.
The formula squares $\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$; it does not cube it.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: $1^3 + 2^3 + \dots + n^3 = \left(1 + 2 + \dots + n\right)^2$.

en.q: The number of terms in $(x+3y)^{16}$:
en.explanation: $(a + b)^n$ has $n + 1$ terms, so $(x + 3y)^{16}$ has 17 terms. The coefficient 3 does not matter.
facts: $(a+b)^n$ has $n + 1$ terms.

en.q: If A.M. and G.M. of two positive numbers are 5 and 3, respectively, find the numbers.
en.explanation:
$a + b = 2 \times 5 = 10$ and $ab = 3^2 = 9$.
So $a, b$ are the roots of $t^2 - 10t + 9 = 0$: 1 and 9.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: Two numbers with AM $A$ and GM $G$ are the roots of $t^2 - 2At + G^2 = 0$.

en.q: The quadratic equation with roots $-4$ and 3 is:
en.explanation:
Sum of roots $= -1$, product $= -12$.
$x^2 - (\text{sum})x + \text{product} = x^2 + x - 12 = 0$, i.e. $(x + 4)(x - 3) = 0$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: Quadratic with roots $\alpha, \beta$: $x^2 - (\alpha + \beta)x + \alpha\beta = 0$.

en.q: If $p$ is a real number and $Q$ is the greatest integer of $p$ then which of the following is always true:
en.explanation:
$Q = [p]$ is the largest integer not exceeding $p$, so $Q \le p$; and $p < Q + 1$, otherwise $Q + 1$ would be a larger such integer.
Equality $Q = p$ happens exactly when $p$ is an integer.

en.q: The number of divisors and the sum of the divisors of the number 45 are, respectively:
notes: 33 is the sum of the proper divisors, leaving out 45.
facts: For $n = p^a q^b$: $\tau(n) = (a+1)(b+1)$ and $\sigma(n) = \frac{p^{a+1}-1}{p-1} \cdot \frac{q^{b+1}-1}{q-1}$.

en.q: How does the Third Principle of Induction differ from the First Principle of Induction?
options: Truth of all previous cases before proving the next is assumed
Cannot be applied in number theory
en.explanation:
First principle: from $P(k)$ alone deduce $P(k + 1)$.
The strong form (called here the third principle) assumes all of $P(1), P(2), \dots, P(k)$ to deduce $P(k + 1)$. It still needs a base case, and it is logically equivalent to the first principle.
notes: It is used widely in number theory, e.g. for prime factorisation.
A base case is still needed.
It is equivalent to ordinary induction.
facts: Strong induction: if $P(1), \dots, P(k)$ together imply $P(k + 1)$, and $P(1)$ holds, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n$.

en.q: If the prime factorization of 2700 is equal to $2^2 3^3 p^a$, then the value of $p - a$ is:
Which of the following number has exactly 12 divisors?
en.explanation:
$90 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$ has $(1 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 12$ divisors.
The others: $70 = 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ has 8; $85 = 5 \cdot 17$ and $86 = 2 \cdot 43$ have 4 each.
facts: $n = p_1^{a_1} \cdots p_k^{a_k}$ has $(a_1 + 1) \cdots (a_k + 1)$ divisors.

en.q: Find the sum and product of roots of a quadratic equation $2x^2 + 6x - 16 = 0$.
options: sum of roots $= 6$, product of roots $= 16$
sum of roots $= 3$, product of roots $= 8$
sum of roots $= -3$, product of roots $= -8$
sum of roots $= -2$, product of roots $= -16$
en.explanation: Sum $= -\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{6}{2} = -3$; product $= \frac{c}{a} = \frac{-16}{2} = -8$.
notes: Signs and the division by $a = 2$ both missed.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$: sum $= -b/a$, product $= c/a$.

en.q: If $p$ and $q$ are roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ then the value of $p^2q + q^2p$ is:
en.explanation: $p^2q + q^2p = pq(p + q) = \frac{c}{a} \cdot \left(-\frac{b}{a}\right) = -\frac{bc}{a^2}$.
notes: Sign and a factor of $a$ missed.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $p^2q + pq^2 = pq(p + q)$: write symmetric expressions in terms of $p + q$ and $pq$.

en.q: The value of the digit $a$ such that the number $84a16$ is divisible by 11 is
en.explanation:
Alternating sum of the digits from the right: $6 - 1 + a - 4 + 8 = 9 + a$.
This must be a multiple of 11, and $a$ is a single digit, so $9 + a = 11$, $a = 2$. Check: $84216 = 11 \times 7656$.
facts: Divisibility by 11: (sum of digits in odd places) − (sum in even places) is a multiple of 11.

en.q: A number is divisible by 11 if:
options: Sum of digits is divisible by 7
Sum of digits is divisible by 11
Difference between sum of digits in odd and even places is divisible by 11
en.explanation: $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$, so a number is congruent mod 11 to the alternating sum of its digits. Hence it is divisible by 11 exactly when (sum of digits in odd places) − (sum in even places) is a multiple of 11. E.g. 121: $1 - 2 + 1 = 0$.
notes: A single digit is never a multiple of 11 except 0.
29 has digit sum 11 but $29$ is not divisible by 11.
facts: Test for 11: alternating digit sum is divisible by 11.

en.q: Which statement is true for coprime $p, q$?
en.explanation:
$\sigma$ (sum of divisors) is multiplicative: when $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, each divisor of $pq$ is uniquely $d_1 d_2$ with $d_1 \mid p$, $d_2 \mid q$, so $\sigma(pq) = \sigma(p)\sigma(q)$.
Check $p = 2$, $q = 3$: $\sigma(6) = 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = 12 = 3 \times 4$.
facts: $\sigma$ and $\tau$ are multiplicative: $f(mn) = f(m)f(n)$ when $\gcd(m, n) = 1$.

en.q: The coefficient of the $4^{\text{th}}$ term in the expansion of $(1 + x)^n$ is 35, then find $n$.
facts: The $(r+1)$th term of $(1 + x)^n$ has coefficient ${}^nC_r$: the 4th term uses ${}^nC_3$.

en.q: When are the two roots of a quadratic equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ said to be equal?
en.explanation: The roots are $\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$; they coincide exactly when the discriminant $b^2 - 4ac = 0$, both equal to $-\frac{b}{2a}$.
notes: The sign of $b$ alone decides nothing.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $D > 0$: distinct real roots; $D = 0$: equal roots; $D < 0$: no real roots.

en.q: What is the value of 'p' if the equation $x^2 + px + 25 = 0$ has real roots?
en.explanation: Real roots need $D = p^2 - 100 \ge 0$, i.e. $p^2 \ge 100$: $|p| \ge 10$ ($p \le -10$ or $p \ge 10$).
notes: For $|p| < 10$ the roots are not real.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: Real roots $\iff b^2 - 4ac \ge 0$.

en.q: If $n = 2^2 * 5^3 * 7$, then what is the number of divisors of $n$?
en.explanation: Number of divisors $= (2 + 1)(3 + 1)(1 + 1) = 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 2 = 24$.
notes: That is the number of distinct primes.
facts: Number of divisors: add 1 to each exponent and multiply.

en.q: The highest common factor (HCF) and the least common multiple (LCM) of the numbers 12, 15, and 21 are, respectively:
en.explanation:
$12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$, $15 = 3 \cdot 5$, $21 = 3 \cdot 7$.
HCF $= 3$ (the only common prime); LCM $= 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 420$.
facts: HCF: lowest powers of common primes; LCM: highest powers of all primes.

en.q: The equation $x^4 - 5x^2 + 4 = 0$ is reducible to a quadratic by substituting:
en.explanation: Only even powers occur, so put $y = x^2$: $y^2 - 5y + 4 = 0$, giving $y = 1$ or $4$ and $x = \pm 1, \pm 2$.
notes: Then $x^2 = \sqrt y$: not a polynomial in $y$.
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $ax^4 + bx^2 + c = 0$ becomes a quadratic in $y = x^2$.

en.q: If $\frac{x}{1 + 9x} + \frac{1 + 9x}{x} = \frac{101}{10}$, then the fraction $\frac{x}{1 + 9x}$ is
en.explanation:
Put $t = \frac{x}{1 + 9x}$: $t + \frac{1}{t} = \frac{101}{10} = 10 + \frac{1}{10}$.
So $t = 10$ or $t = \frac{1}{10}$; only $\frac{1}{10}$ is offered (it comes from $x = 1$).
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations
facts: $t + \frac1t = k + \frac1k \Rightarrow t = k$ or $t = \frac1k$.

en.q: The quadratic equation corresponding to the roots $1 + \sqrt{3}$ and $1 - \sqrt{3}$ is:
path: 1.8 Quadratic equations and theory of equations

en.q: On the unit circle, the coordinates of point are $(x, y) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. If $\theta = 300^\circ$, what is $x$?
en.explanation: $x = \cos 300^\circ = \cos(360^\circ - 60^\circ) = \cos 60^\circ = \frac12$ (fourth quadrant: cosine positive).
notes: More than 1: impossible on the unit circle.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: $\cos(360^\circ - \theta) = \cos\theta$, $\sin(360^\circ - \theta) = -\sin\theta$.

en.q: If $\theta$ lies in quadrant II, the signs of $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta)$ are
en.explanation: In quadrant II the point $(\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$ has $x < 0$, $y > 0$: $\sin\theta > 0$, $\cos\theta < 0$. E.g. $\theta = 120^\circ$: $(\sin\theta, \cos\theta) = \left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}, -\frac12\right)$, signs $(+, -)$.
notes: ASTC: only sine is positive in II.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: ASTC: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine are positive in quadrants I, II, III, IV.

en.q: Which of the following is the equation of line which passes through the intersection of $x + y - 1 = 0$ and $2x + 3y - 5 = 0$ and parallel to $y$-axis?
en.explanation:
From $x + y = 1$ and $2x + 3y = 5$: $y = 3$, $x = -2$.
A line parallel to the $y$-axis is $x = \text{constant}$, so $x = -2$.
facts: Line parallel to the $y$-axis through $(h, k)$: $x = h$.

en.q: Find the radius of the circle in which a central angle of $30^\circ$ intercepts an arc of length 32 cm.
en.explanation:
$\theta = 30^\circ = \frac{\pi}{6}$ and $l = r\theta$, so $r = \frac{32}{\pi/6} = \frac{192}{\pi}$.
With $\pi \approx 3.14$: $r \approx 61.15$ cm.
notes: Arc length equals radius only for 1 radian.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: $l = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians.

en.q: The equation of the directrix of the conic section $y^2 - 6y - 4x + 1 = 0$ is
en.explanation:
Complete the square: $(y - 3)^2 = 4x + 8 = 4(x + 2)$. Parabola with vertex $(-2, 3)$, $a = 1$, opening to the right.
Directrix: $x = -2 - 1 = -3$, i.e. $x + 3 = 0$.
facts: $(y - k)^2 = 4a(x - h)$: focus $(h + a, k)$, directrix $x = h - a$.

en.q: In a plane triangle, if $a, b$ and $c$ are the lengths of the sides of $\triangle ABC$ and are in Arithmetic Progression, then $a\cos^2\left(\frac{C}{2}\right) + c\cos^2\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)$, (where, $A$ and $C$ are angles in $\triangle ABC$), is equal to:
en.explanation:
$\cos^2\frac{C}{2} = \frac{1 + \cos C}{2}$, so the expression is $\frac{a + c}{2} + \frac{a\cos C + c\cos A}{2}$.
Projection rule: $a\cos C + c\cos A = b$. So it equals $\frac{a + b + c}{2} = \frac{3b}{2}$, since $a + c = 2b$.
notes: The AP is used with the wrong side.
facts: $a\cos^2\frac{C}{2} + c\cos^2\frac{A}{2} = s$, the semi-perimeter, in every triangle.

en.q: Which of the following is the graph of $\sin(2x)$?
options: Graph: a wave of amplitude 1 and period $2\pi$, at its maximum 1 at $x = 0$
Graph: a wave of amplitude 1 and period $\pi$, at its maximum 1 at $x = 0$
Graph: a wave of amplitude 1 and period $\pi$, through the origin and rising there
Graph: a wave of amplitude 1 and period $2\pi$, through the origin and rising there
en.explanation: $\sin 2x$ has amplitude 1 and period $\frac{2\pi}{2} = \pi$. At $x = 0$ it is 0 and increasing, with zeros at multiples of $\frac{\pi}{2}$ and peaks at $\frac{\pi}{4} + n\pi$. Only graph (c) fits.
notes: This is $\cos 2x$: right period, but $\sin 2x = 0$ at $x = 0$.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: $\sin kx$ and $\cos kx$ have period $\frac{2\pi}{k}$.

en.q: The eccentricity of the hyperbola $36x^2 - 64y^2 = 1$ is:
notes: Less than 1: impossible for a hyperbola.
Less than 1: impossible for a hyperbola.
facts: Hyperbola: $e^2 = 1 + \frac{b^2}{a^2} > 1$.

en.q: Find the equation of the line that passes through $(-1, 5)$ with slope $-2$.
facts: Point–slope form: $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$.

en.q: Which of the following pairs of angles are coterminal?
en.explanation:
Coterminal angles differ by a multiple of $360^\circ$: $30^\circ - (-330^\circ) = 360^\circ$.
The other pairs differ by $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ and $240^\circ$.
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: $\theta$ and $\theta + 360^\circ k$ are coterminal.

en.q: The value of $\cos\left(\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\right)$ is equal to
en.explanation: Let $\theta = \sin^{-1}\frac{5}{13}$, so $\theta \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Then $\cos\theta = \sqrt{1 - \frac{25}{169}} = \frac{12}{13}$ (positive in this range).
notes: More than 1: impossible for a cosine.
More than 1: impossible for a cosine.

en.q: Find the magnitude of $\vec a$ given by $\vec a = (\vec i - 3\vec j + 2\vec k) \times (-\vec i + \vec j + 3\vec k)$
en.explanation:
$$\vec a = \begin{vmatrix} \vec i & \vec j & \vec k \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -11\vec i - 5\vec j - 2\vec k$$
(components: $-9 - 2 = -11$, $-(3 + 2) = -5$, $1 - 3 = -2$).
$|\vec a| = \sqrt{121 + 25 + 4} = \sqrt{150}$.
facts: $|\vec u \times \vec v|^2 = |\vec u|^2|\vec v|^2 - (\vec u \cdot \vec v)^2$: here $14 \cdot 11 - 2^2 = 150$.

en.q: The equation $\frac{x^2}{4} - \frac{y^2}{16} = 1$ represents:
en.explanation: It has the form $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ (squares with opposite signs): a hyperbola with $a = 2$, $b = 4$.
notes: An ellipse has a $+$ between the squares.
A circle needs equal coefficients with the same sign.
A parabola has only one squared variable.
facts: Opposite signs on $x^2$ and $y^2$: hyperbola; same signs: ellipse or circle.

en.q: If a line $x - y = 4$ has $d$ distance from the point $(-3, 5)$ then the value of $d$ is:
notes: Uses $|-3 - 5 + 4| = 4$: sign of the constant slipped.
facts: Distance from $(x_1, y_1)$ to $ax + by + c = 0$: $\frac{|ax_1 + by_1 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}$.

en.q: The equation of the line passing through the point of intersection of $x + y - 5 = 0$ and $2x - y - 7 = 0$ and making an angle of $45^\circ$ with the X axis is:
en.explanation:
Adding the equations: $3x = 12$, $x = 4$, $y = 1$. Slope $= \tan 45^\circ = 1$.
$y - 1 = x - 4$, i.e. $x - y - 3 = 0$.
notes: Slope $-1$, and $(4, 1)$ is not on it.
Slope $-1$, and $(4, 1)$ is not on it.
Slope 1, but $(4, 1)$ is not on it.
facts: Angle $\theta$ with the $x$-axis means slope $\tan\theta$.

en.q: Find the equation of straight line upon which the length of perpendicular from origin is $4\sqrt{2}$ units and this perpendicular makes an angle $75^\circ$ with the positive direction of $x$-axis.
en.explanation:
Normal form: $x\cos 75^\circ + y\sin 75^\circ = 4\sqrt2$, with $\cos 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt3 - 1}{2\sqrt2}$ and $\sin 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt3 + 1}{2\sqrt2}$.
Multiply by $2\sqrt2$: $(\sqrt3 - 1)x + (\sqrt3 + 1)y = 16$.
notes: Equal coefficients mean the perpendicular is at $45^\circ$.
Equal coefficients mean the perpendicular is at $45^\circ$.
Swaps $\cos$ and $\sin$ (that is $15^\circ$) and doubles the constant.
facts: Normal form: $x\cos\alpha + y\sin\alpha = p$; $\cos 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt3 - 1}{2\sqrt2}$.

en.q: Domain and range of $\sin(x)$ are ________, respectively.
en.explanation: $\sin x$ is defined for every real $x$, and it takes every value from $-1$ to $1$, including $\pm 1$ (at $x = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$).
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: $\sin x$: domain $\mathbb{R}$, range $[-1, 1]$.

en.q: What is the conversion of $\frac{11}{16}$ radians into degree?
en.explanation: $\frac{11}{16} \times \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} = \frac{123.75^\circ}{\pi} \approx 39.4^\circ$ (with $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$: $39.375^\circ$).
path: 9.1 Trigonometric ratios and the unit circle
facts: 1 radian $= \frac{180^\circ}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$.

en.q: Find the equation in standard form of a straight line that passes through the points $(1, 3)$ and $(-2, 4)$.
facts: Check a line by substituting both given points.

en.q: If the vectors $\vec a$ and $\vec b$ are perpendicular with $|\vec a| = 5$ and $|\vec b| = 12$, then $|\vec a + \vec b|$ is equal to :
en.explanation: $|\vec a + \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2 + |\vec b|^2 + 2\vec a \cdot \vec b = 25 + 144 + 0 = 169$, so $|\vec a + \vec b| = 13$.
notes: $5 + 12$ holds only for vectors in the same direction.
facts: For perpendicular vectors $|\vec a \pm \vec b|^2 = |\vec a|^2 + |\vec b|^2$.

en.q: The standard deviation of a sample of 20 observations is 5. If a constant value 2 is added to each observation, then the standard deviation of the resultant sample is:
en.explanation: Adding a constant shifts every observation and the mean by the same amount, so the deviations from the mean, and hence the SD, are unchanged: 5.
notes: $5 \times 2$: that happens when each value is multiplied by 2.
SD is unchanged by a shift of origin.
facts: SD is unaffected by a change of origin but scales with a change of scale.

en.q: Given that the radius of a circle is increasing at a constant rate of 1 cm/s. what is the instantaneous rate at which the circle's area is increasing at the moment the radius measures 5 cm?
en.explanation: $A = \pi r^2$, so $\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r \frac{dr}{dt} = 2\pi \times 5 \times 1 = 10\pi \text{ cm}^2/\text{s}$.
facts: $\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}$: the rate of change of area is circumference × rate of radius.

en.q: The slope of the normal to the curve $y = x^{x + 2}$ at $x = 1$ is
en.explanation:
$\ln y = (x + 2)\ln x$, so $\frac{y'}{y} = \ln x + \frac{x + 2}{x}$.
At $x = 1$: $y = 1$ and $y' = 1 \times (0 + 3) = 3$. Normal slope $= -\frac{1}{y'} = -\frac13$.
facts: Slope of normal $= -\frac{1}{dy/dx}$; differentiate $x^{f(x)}$ by taking logs.

en.q: If $a = 2i + 3j$, $b = i - j$, then $a - b$ is:
facts: Vectors add and subtract componentwise; watch the signs.

en.q: The integrating factor for the linear differential equation $(1 + x^2)\frac{dy}{dx} + 2xy = \cot(x)$, $(x \ne 0)$, is:
en.explanation:
Standard form: $\frac{dy}{dx} + \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}y = \frac{\cot x}{1 + x^2}$.
IF $= e^{\int \frac{2x}{1 + x^2}dx} = e^{\ln(1 + x^2)} = 1 + x^2$.
notes: This is $\int P\,dx$, before taking $e$ to that power.
A constant multiple works but is not the standard IF.
Exponent should be $\ln(1 + x^2)$, not $1 + x^2$.
facts: For $y' + Py = Q$, IF $= e^{\int P\,dx}$.

en.q: Find the shortest distance between the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ whose vector equations are: $\vec r = 2\hat i + 3\hat j + \lambda(\hat i - 2\hat j + 2\hat k)$, $\vec r = 3\hat i + 4\hat j - 4\hat k + \mu(2\hat i - 6\hat j + \hat k)$.
notes: $\frac{|(\vec a_2 - \vec a_1) \cdot (\vec b_1 \times \vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1 \times \vec b_2|}$.
The lines are skew, not intersecting.
Sign slip in the dot product: $10 + 3 - 2$.
facts: SD between skew lines $= \frac{|(\vec a_2 - \vec a_1) \cdot (\vec b_1 \times \vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1 \times \vec b_2|}$.

en.q: If $\vec a = (0, -1, 2)$, $\vec b = (1, 0, -1)$ and $\vec c = (2, -1, 0)$ then which of the following is the unit vector parallel to $\vec a - \vec b + \vec c$.
notes: Not even a unit vector: its length is $\sqrt{14/20}$.
facts: Unit vector along $\vec v$: $\frac{\vec v}{|\vec v|}$.

en.q: The equation of a plane in OXYZ plane is:
options: linear in x, y and z
quadratic in x, y and linear in z
Cubic in x, y, and z
quadratic in x, y, and z
en.explanation: Every plane has an equation $ax + by + cz + d = 0$ with $a, b, c$ not all zero: a first-degree (linear) equation in $x, y, z$. Conversely, every such equation is a plane.
notes: $z = x^2 + y^2$ is a paraboloid, not a plane.
Second-degree equations give spheres, cones and other quadrics.
facts: Planes are exactly the first-degree equations in $x, y, z$.

en.q: If 45 degree angle is made by a line with x-axis and y-axis then the angle of this line with z-axis in degrees is_______
en.explanation: $\cos^2\alpha + \cos^2\beta + \cos^2\gamma = 1$: $\frac12 + \frac12 + \cos^2\gamma = 1$, so $\cos\gamma = 0$ and $\gamma = 90^\circ$.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Direction cosines satisfy $l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$.

en.q: Find the angle between the pair of lines given by: $\vec r=\hat i-2\hat j-4\hat k+\lambda(-2\hat i+2\hat j+\hat k)$ and $\vec r=4\hat i+\hat j-3\hat k+\mu(2\hat i+6\hat j-3\hat k)$.
en.explanation: Direction vectors: $\vec b_1=(-2,2,1)$ and $\vec b_2=(2,6,-3)$. $\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=-4+12-3=5$, $|\vec b_1|=3$, $|\vec b_2|=7$. So $\cos\theta=\frac{5}{3\cdot7}=\frac{5}{21}$ and $\theta=\cos^{-1}\frac{5}{21}$.
notes: The direction vectors are not proportional, so the lines are not parallel.
Wrong value of the dot product.
Wrong value of the dot product.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: The angle between two lines depends only on their direction vectors: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2|}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|}$.

en.q: The direction cosines of the line joining the points $(1, 3, -4)$ and $(3, 2, -8)$ are:
en.explanation: Direction ratios: $(3-1,\ 2-3,\ -8+4)=(2,-1,-4)$. Their length is $\sqrt{4+1+16}=\sqrt{21}$. Dividing, the direction cosines are $\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{21}},-\frac{1}{\sqrt{21}},-\frac{4}{\sqrt{21}}\right)$.
notes: These are direction ratios, not cosines: their squares do not add to 1.
The signs of the second and third ratios are dropped.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Direction cosines $=$ direction ratios divided by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$; their squares add to 1.

en.q: The function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ given by $f(x)=x^3$ is:
en.explanation: $f'(x)=3x^2\ge0$, and it is zero only at $x=0$. Directly: $x_1<x_2\Rightarrow x_1^3<x_2^3$. So $x^3$ is (strictly) increasing on $\mathbb{R}$.
facts: If $f'\ge0$ and $f'=0$ only at isolated points, $f$ is strictly increasing.

en.q: Find the vector equation for the line passing through the points $(2, 1, 5)$ and $(4, 5, 7)$.
options: $2\hat i+\hat j+5\hat k+\lambda(2\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k)$
$2\hat i+\hat j+5\hat k+\lambda(4\hat i+\hat j+6\hat k)$
$2\hat i+\hat j+5\hat k+\lambda(3\hat i+2\hat j+5\hat k)$
$2\hat i+\hat j+5\hat k+\lambda(-2\hat i+4\hat j-2\hat k)$
en.explanation: $\vec r=\vec a+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$ with $\vec a=(2,1,5)$, $\vec b=(4,5,7)$. $\vec b-\vec a=(2,4,2)$, so $\vec r=2\hat i+\hat j+5\hat k+\lambda(2\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k)$.
notes: Direction not parallel to $\vec b-\vec a=(2,4,2)$.
path: 13.1 Direction cosines and the straight line
facts: Line through $A$ and $B$: $\vec r=\vec a+\lambda(\vec b-\vec a)$.

en.q: If $\theta$ be the angle between the planes $x+2y+2z=0$ and $2x-y+2z=0$, then the value of $\cos(\theta)$ is
en.explanation: The normals are $(1,2,2)$ and $(2,-1,2)$, each of length 3. $\cos\theta=\frac{|1\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)+2\cdot2|}{3\cdot3}=\frac{4}{9}$.
notes: The angle between planes is taken acute, so $\cos\theta\ge0$.
facts: Angle between planes $=$ angle between their normals: $\cos\theta=\frac{|\vec n_1\cdot\vec n_2|}{|\vec n_1||\vec n_2|}$.

en.q: If $\vec F=6\hat i-3\hat j+2\hat k$ be a force acting on a point P whose position vector is $\vec r=2\hat i+2\hat j-\hat k$, then the moment of $\vec F$ which is $\vec r\times\vec F$ about the origin is:
en.explanation: $\vec r\times\vec F=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&2&-1\\6&-3&2\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(4-3)-\hat j(4+6)+\hat k(-6-12)=\hat i-10\hat j-18\hat k$.
notes: Multiplies the components instead of taking the cross product.
Sign slip in the $\hat j$ term.
Mixes component products with the cross product.
facts: Moment of a force about O: $\vec M=\vec r\times\vec F$, found as a $3\times3$ determinant.

en.q: If $f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x+1$, then local maximum and minimum values of $f(x)$ are
notes: 3 is where the minimum occurs, not the maximum value.
facts: At a stationary point, $f''<0$ gives a local maximum and $f''>0$ a local minimum.

en.q: The function $f(x)=(x+1)(x-2)^2$ has a local minimum at:
en.explanation: $f'(x)=(x-2)^2+2(x+1)(x-2)=(x-2)\cdot3x$, so the stationary points are $0$ and $2$. $f''(x)=6x-6$: $f''(0)=-6<0$ (maximum), $f''(2)=6>0$ (minimum). So the local minimum is at $x=2$.
notes: $x=-1$ is a root, not a stationary point.
facts: A squared factor $(x-a)^2$ times a positive factor gives a local minimum at $x=a$.

en.q: The magnitude of $3\hat i-4\hat j$ is:
notes: Only the zero vector has magnitude 0.
facts: $|a\hat i+b\hat j+c\hat k|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2+c^2}$.

en.q: If $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+3\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i-\hat j+\hat k$, then $\vec a\times\vec b$ is
en.explanation: $\vec a\times\vec b=\hat i(2\cdot1-3\cdot(-1))-\hat j(1\cdot1-3\cdot2)+\hat k(1\cdot(-1)-2\cdot2)=5\hat i+5\hat j-5\hat k$. Check: $(5,5,-5)\cdot(1,2,3)=0$ and $(5,5,-5)\cdot(2,-1,1)=0$.
notes: Sign errors in the $\hat j$ and $\hat k$ terms.
Sign error in the $\hat j$ term.
Sign error in the $\hat k$ term.
facts: A cross product must be perpendicular to both vectors: check with two dot products.

en.q: Which of the following are required to calculate the standard deviation of grouped data?
en.explanation: For grouped data $\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum f_ix_i^2}{N}-\left(\frac{\sum f_ix_i}{N}\right)^2}$, where the $x_i$ are class mid-points (from the class intervals) and the $f_i$ are frequencies. Both are needed.
notes: Without frequencies the weights are unknown.
Without the classes there are no values $x_i$.
facts: Grouped SD uses the class mid-points weighted by the frequencies.

en.q: If range of a data is given 24 and all observations are increased by 10, then new range will be_______
en.explanation: Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest. Adding 10 to every observation adds 10 to both, so the range stays $24$.
notes: A shift of origin does not change the range.
facts: Range, QD, MD and SD do not change when the same number is added to every observation.

en.q: Which of the following statements about variance of grouped data is true?
options: Variance can be negative for some data sets.
Variance is independent of the units of the data.
Variance measures the degree to which the data values differ from the mean.
Variance is always equal to the square root of mean deviation.
en.explanation: Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean, $\frac1N\sum f(x-\bar x)^2$, so it measures how far the values spread from the mean. It is never negative, its unit is the square of the data's unit, and it is the square of the SD (it has no fixed link with the mean deviation).
notes: A mean of squares is never negative.
Its unit is the square of the data's unit.
Variance $=\sigma^2$; the mean deviation is a different measure.
facts: Variance $=\frac1N\sum f(x-\bar x)^2\ge0$, in squared units.

en.q: What will be the range and standard deviation of a data set having all data entries equal?
en.explanation: If every value is $c$, the largest and smallest are both $c$, so the range is $0$; every deviation $x_i-\bar x$ is $0$, so the SD is $0$.
facts: SD $=0$ exactly when all observations are equal.

en.q: The solution of $\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{-y}(e^x+x^2)$ is:
en.explanation: Separate the variables: $e^y\,dy=(e^x+x^2)\,dx$. Integrate: $e^y=e^x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c$.
facts: Variables separable: collect $y$ with $dy$ and $x$ with $dx$, then integrate both sides.

en.q: Consider positive numbers $a_1\ge a_2\ge a_3$ and $b_1\ge b_2\ge b_3$. If $\sum a_i=12$ and $\sum b_i=18$, then the minimum possible value of $a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3$ according to Chebyshev’s inequality is:
en.explanation: Chebyshev's sum inequality for two sequences ordered the same way: $\frac1n\sum a_ib_i\ge\left(\frac1n\sum a_i\right)\left(\frac1n\sum b_i\right)$. With $n=3$: $\sum a_ib_i\ge\frac{12\times18}{3}=72$. Equality holds when all $a_i$ are equal, e.g. $a_i=4$, $b_i=6$, so 72 is the minimum.
path: 1.6 Sequences and series: AP, GP, HP
facts: Chebyshev: if $a_i$ and $b_i$ are similarly ordered, $n\sum a_ib_i\ge\left(\sum a_i\right)\left(\sum b_i\right)$.

en.q: The solution of the inequality $\frac{x-10}{5}<\frac{x-7}{7}$ when $x$ is a real number is:
en.explanation: Multiply by 35 (positive, so the sign stays): $7(x-10)<5(x-7)$, i.e. $7x-70<5x-35$, so $2x<35$ and $x<17.5$.
notes: No lower bound comes out of the working.
No lower bound comes out of the working.
facts: Multiplying an inequality by a positive number keeps its direction.

en.q: For which values of $x\in\mathbb{R}$, the inequality $4-2x>10$ holds?
en.explanation: $-2x>6$. Dividing by $-2$ reverses the inequality: $x<-3$.
notes: Forgot to reverse the sign when dividing by $-2$.
facts: Dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses it.

en.q: A class interval of a continuous type data is $15-27$. What is the class width?
en.explanation: Class width $=$ upper limit $-$ lower limit $=27-15=12$.
facts: Class width (size) $=$ upper class limit $-$ lower class limit.

en.q: If the coefficient of variation of two distributions are 60 and 70 and also the mean are 20 and 10, respectively, then the standard deviation of both distributions are_____.
en.explanation: CV $=\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100$, so $\sigma=\frac{\text{CV}\times\bar x}{100}$: $\sigma_1=\frac{60\times20}{100}=12$ and $\sigma_2=\frac{70\times10}{100}=7$.
facts: Coefficient of variation $=\frac{\sigma}{\bar x}\times100$.

en.q: The solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x$, given that $y(1)=7$ is
facts: Use the initial condition to fix the constant of integration.

en.q: Identify the interval of $x$ for which the inequality $-3\le4-\frac{7x}{2}\le18$ holds.
en.explanation: Subtract 4: $-7\le-\frac{7x}{2}\le14$. Multiply by $-\frac27$, which reverses both signs: $2\ge x\ge-4$. So $x\in[-4,2]$.
facts: In a double inequality, multiplying by a negative number reverses both signs.

en.q: The solution of the differential equation $x(1+y^2)dx+y(1+x^2)dy=0$ is:
en.explanation: Divide by $(1+x^2)(1+y^2)$: $\frac{x\,dx}{1+x^2}+\frac{y\,dy}{1+y^2}=0$. Integrate: $\frac12\log(1+x^2)+\frac12\log(1+y^2)=$ constant, i.e. $(1+x^2)(1+y^2)=c$.
notes: That would need $\frac{dx}{1+x^2}$; here the numerator has an extra $x$.
The logarithms add, they do not subtract.
Wrong sign inside the first factor.
facts: $\int\frac{x\,dx}{1+x^2}=\frac12\log(1+x^2)$.

en.q: The solution of the inequality $\frac{x}{2}\ge\frac{5x-2}{3}-\frac{7x-3}{5}$ is:
en.explanation: Multiply by 30: $15x\ge10(5x-2)-6(7x-3)=8x-2$. So $7x\ge-2$, i.e. $x\ge-\frac27$.
facts: Clear the denominators with their LCM (a positive number) before solving.

en.q: The standard deviation of a data set is zero when:
en.explanation: $\sigma^2=\frac1n\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$ is a sum of squares, so it is 0 only when every $x_i=\bar x$: all values are equal.
notes: Negative values can still be spread out.
Positive values can still be spread out.
facts: $\sigma=0$ if and only if all observations are equal.

en.q: The solution of the inequality $1\le\frac{9x+15}{3}\le7$ is:
en.explanation: Multiply by 3: $3\le9x+15\le21$. Subtract 15: $-12\le9x\le6$. Divide by 9: $-\frac43\le x\le\frac23$.
facts: Apply each step to all three parts of a double inequality.

en.q: The weights (in kg) of 50 students are distributed as: Weight (kg): $x-40$, $40-50$, $50-60$, $60-70$, $70-80$; Frequency: 5, 10, 15, 12, 8. If the range of the data is 45 kg, then value of $x$ is:
en.explanation: For grouped data, range $=$ upper limit of the last class $-$ lower limit of the first class $=80-x$. So $80-x=45$ and $x=35$.
facts: Range of grouped data $=$ upper limit of the highest class $-$ lower limit of the lowest class.

en.q: The general solution of the differential equation $y'=y$ with $a$ as arbitrary constant is:
en.explanation: $\frac{dy}{y}=dx\Rightarrow\log y=x+c\Rightarrow y=ae^x$.
facts: $y'=ky$ has general solution $y=ae^{kx}$.

en.q: The particular solution of $\frac{dy}{dx}=3x^2$, $y(1)=4$:
facts: A particular solution is the general solution with the constant fixed by the condition.

en.q: The principal value of $(-i)^i$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$ is:
en.explanation: Principal $\log(-i)=\log1+i\left(-\frac\pi2\right)=-\frac{i\pi}{2}$. So $(-i)^i=e^{i\log(-i)}=e^{i\cdot(-i\pi/2)}=e^{\pi/2}$.
notes: $\frac\pi2$ is the exponent, not the value.
facts: $z^w=e^{w\log z}$, principal value with $\arg z\in(-\pi,\pi]$; e.g. $i^i=e^{-\pi/2}$ and $(-i)^i=e^{\pi/2}$.

en.q: The differential equation corresponding to the equation $y^2=4ax$, where $a$ is arbitrary constant, is:
en.explanation: Differentiate: $2yy'=4a$. Substitute $4a=2yy'$ in $y^2=4ax$: $y^2=2xyy'$, i.e. $y=2xy'$.
notes: The factor 2 is on the wrong side.
facts: To form a DE, differentiate once per arbitrary constant and eliminate the constants.

en.q: The inequality $|x|\ge5$ implies
en.explanation: $|x|\ge5$ says $x$ is at distance at least 5 from 0: $x\le-5$ or $x\ge5$.
facts: For $a>0$: $|x|\ge a\iff x\le-a$ or $x\ge a$; $|x|\le a\iff-a\le x\le a$.

en.q: The value of the range for the data 4, 9, 14, 20, is
en.explanation: Range $=$ largest $-$ smallest $=20-4=16$.
facts: Range $=$ largest value $-$ smallest value.

en.q: Which of the following condition is sufficient for a function $f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)$ to be analytic on a domain D ?
options: u and v are continuous in D and satisfy CR equations in D
u and v satisfy CR equations in D
u and v are differentiable in D
u and v are continuously differentiable in D and satisfy CR equations in D
en.explanation: The Cauchy–Riemann equations $u_x=v_y$, $u_y=-v_x$ are necessary but not sufficient on their own. If in addition the first partial derivatives of $u$ and $v$ are continuous in D, then $f$ is analytic in D.
notes: Continuity of $u$ and $v$ is not enough; their partial derivatives must be continuous.
CR alone is not enough: $\sqrt{|xy|}$ satisfies them at the origin but is not differentiable there.
Without CR it fails, e.g. $f=\bar z$.
facts: Sufficient condition for analyticity: continuous first partial derivatives plus the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

en.q: The integral $\int_{|z|=2}\frac{\cos z}{z^3}\,dz$ equals
en.explanation: Cauchy's integral formula: $\oint\frac{f(z)}{z^3}dz=\frac{2\pi i}{2!}f''(0)$ with $f=\cos z$, $f''(0)=-\cos0=-1$. So the integral is $\pi i\cdot(-1)=-\pi i$.
path: 10.11 Important results and exam tips: complex numbers
facts: $\oint\frac{f(z)}{(z-a)^{n+1}}dz=\frac{2\pi i}{n!}f^{(n)}(a)$ for $a$ inside the contour.

en.q: The value of Integral $\int_1^2\int_0^{y/2}y\,dx\,dy$ is:
en.explanation:
The paper prints the differentials as $y\,dy\,dx$, but the inner upper limit $\frac y2$ contains $y$, so the inner variable must be $x$: the integral is read as $\int_1^2\int_0^{y/2}y\,dx\,dy$ (this gives the key).
Inner integral in $x$: $\int_0^{y/2}y\,dx=\frac{y^2}{2}$. Outer: $\int_1^2\frac{y^2}{2}dy=\frac{8-1}{6}=\frac76$.
facts: In an iterated integral, the inner limits may depend only on the outer variable.

en.q: Evaluate $\int_0^1\int_y^1\exp(x^2)\,dx\,dy$
en.explanation: $e^{x^2}$ has no elementary antiderivative, so change the order. The region is $0\le y\le x\le1$: $\int_0^1\int_0^x e^{x^2}dy\,dx=\int_0^1xe^{x^2}dx=\frac12\left[e^{x^2}\right]_0^1=\frac12(e-1)$.
notes: Sign slip at the lower limit.
Forgets the $-1$ from the lower limit.
facts: Change the order of integration when the inner integral is not elementary.

en.q: Let $f(z)=\begin{cases}\frac{z^2}{|z|}, & z\ne0\\0, & z=0\end{cases}$ where $z=x+iy\in\mathbb{C}$. Which of the following statements is true about the continuity of $f(z)$ at $z=0$
options: $f(z)$ is continuous only along the real axis
$f(z)$ is continuous at $z=0$, since $\lim_{z\to0}f(z)=0$ along all paths
$f(z)$ is not continuous at $z=0$, since the limit depends on the direction of approach
$f(z)$ is continuous only along the imaginary axis
en.explanation:
The paper prints the numerator as 'z2'; it is read as $z^2$ (a lost superscript; the key agrees).
$|f(z)-0|=\frac{|z|^2}{|z|}=|z|\to0$ as $z\to0$, whatever the path. So $\lim_{z\to0}f(z)=0=f(0)$: $f$ is continuous at 0. (Read literally as $\frac{2z}{|z|}$, $f$ would have modulus 2 near 0 and no limit, which is option (c).)
notes: The limit is 0 along every path, not just the real axis.
That happens for $\frac{z}{|z|}$ or $\frac{z^2}{|z|^2}$, not here.
The limit is 0 along every path.
facts: If $|f(z)-L|\le g(|z|)$ with $g(r)\to0$, then $f(z)\to L$ along every path.

en.q: If $z=i\pi$, then the value of $e^z$ is
en.explanation: Euler: $e^{i\pi}=\cos\pi+i\sin\pi=-1$.
path: 10.4 Polar form, Euler's form and De Moivre's theorem
facts: $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$; $e^{i\pi}=-1$.

en.q: The mean deviation of the data about the mean is zero if:
options: All entries in the data are negative
All entries in the data are same
All entries in the data are positive
All entries in the data are distinct
en.explanation: MD $=\frac1n\sum|x_i-\bar x|$ is a sum of non-negative terms, so it is 0 only when every $x_i=\bar x$: all entries are the same.
notes: Negative entries can still be spread out.
Positive entries can still be spread out.
Distinct entries make the MD positive.
facts: Mean deviation is 0 only for constant data.

en.q: For the function $f(z)=u(x,y)+iv(x,y)=x^2-y^2+i(2xy)$, which of the following statements is true regarding the Cauchy–Riemann equations
options: The Cauchy–Riemann equations are satisfied everywhere except on the line $x=0$
The Cauchy–Riemann equations are satisfied only at $(0,0)$
The Cauchy–Riemann equations are satisfied at all points, hence $f(z)$ is analytic everywhere
The Cauchy–Riemann equations are not satisfied at any point
en.explanation: $u_x=2x=v_y$ and $u_y=-2y=-v_x$ at every point, and these partials are continuous. In fact $f(z)=z^2$, which is entire.
facts: $z^2=(x^2-y^2)+i\,2xy$ is analytic everywhere.

en.q: Which one of the following is a measure of dispersion?
en.explanation: Quartile deviation $\frac{Q_3-Q_1}{2}$ measures spread. HM, AM and GM are averages (measures of central tendency).
facts: Measures of dispersion: range, quartile deviation, mean deviation, standard deviation.

en.q: What is correct value of $\Gamma\left(-\frac12\right)$?
en.explanation: From $\Gamma(x+1)=x\Gamma(x)$ with $x=-\frac12$: $\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)=-\frac12\Gamma\left(-\frac12\right)$, so $\Gamma\left(-\frac12\right)=-2\Gamma\left(\frac12\right)=-2\sqrt\pi$.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: $\Gamma(x)=\frac{\Gamma(x+1)}{x}$ extends $\Gamma$ to negative non-integers.

en.q: If $f(z)=\frac{z-2}{z}$ and C is the semi circle $z=3e^{i\theta}$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, then $\int_C f(z)\,dz=$ _____.
en.explanation: $f(z)=1-\frac2z$. Along C, $z$ runs from $3$ to $-3$, so $\int_C dz=-3-3=-6$. On $z=3e^{i\theta}$, $\frac{dz}{z}=i\,d\theta$, so $\int_C\frac{dz}{z}=i\pi$. Hence $\int_C f\,dz=-6-2\pi i$.
notes: Sign of $\int_C dz$ wrong: it is $-3-3$.
path: 10.11 Important results and exam tips: complex numbers
facts: On $z=re^{i\theta}$, $\frac{dz}{z}=i\,d\theta$; and $\int_C dz=$ end point $-$ start point.

notes: The integrand decays like $\frac1{x^2}$, so the integral converges.
facts: $\int\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\tan^{-1}x$; $\tan^{-1}x\to\frac\pi2$ as $x\to\infty$.

en.q: Evaluate the double integral over the region bounded by the circle $x^2+y^2\le a^2$: $I=\iint(x^2+y^2)\,dx\,dy$
en.explanation: Polar coordinates: $I=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^a r^2\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot\frac{a^4}{4}=\frac{\pi a^4}{2}$.
notes: That is the area of the disc.
facts: In polar coordinates $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$.

en.q: The value of $\sin^{-1}(-i)$ is:
en.explanation: $\sin^{-1}z=-i\log\left(iz+\sqrt{1-z^2}\right)$. With $z=-i$: $iz=1$ and $\sqrt{1-z^2}=\pm\sqrt2$. So $\sin^{-1}(-i)=-i\log(1\pm\sqrt2)$. Check: $\sin(-iy)=-i\sinh y$ and $\sinh\log(1+\sqrt2)=1$.
path: 10.10 Inverse circular and inverse hyperbolic functions
facts: $\sin^{-1}z=-i\log\left(iz+\sqrt{1-z^2}\right)$.

en.q: Which of the following relations is true?
en.explanation:
Here $r,\theta$ are the polar coordinates of $(x,y)$: $x=r\cos\theta$, $y=r\sin\theta$. The Jacobian is $\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}=\begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta&-r\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&r\cos\theta\end{vmatrix}=r$, so $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$ and (d) is right.
Option (b) evaluates $f$ at $(r\sin\theta,r\cos\theta)$, the mirror image of the point in the line $y=x$; it would only be right for a different angle (measured from the $y$-axis), not for the usual polar $\theta$.
notes: Swaps $\sin$ and $\cos$: with the usual polar $\theta$ this evaluates $f$ at the wrong point.
facts: Polar coordinates: $dx\,dy=r\,dr\,d\theta$ (the Jacobian is $r$).

en.q: The value of improper integral $\int_1^\infty\frac{1}{x^{3/2}}\,dx$ is:
facts: $\int_1^\infty\frac{dx}{x^p}=\frac{1}{p-1}$ for $p>1$, divergent for $p\le1$.

en.q: If matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&3\\1&3&-3\\-2&-4&-4\end{bmatrix}$, then the value of $\frac{8A}{\text{Determinant}(A)}$ is equal to:
facts: Expand a $3\times3$ determinant along the first row, watching the alternating signs.

en.q: The fixed points of $f(z)=\frac{2iz+5}{z-2i}$ are:
en.explanation: Fixed points: $z=\frac{2iz+5}{z-2i}\Rightarrow z^2-2iz=2iz+5\Rightarrow z^2-4iz-5=0$. So $z=\frac{4i\pm\sqrt{-16+20}}{2}=2i\pm1$.
path: 10.5 Square root of a complex number
facts: Fixed points of $w=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$ solve $cz^2+(d-a)z-b=0$.

en.q: For what value of K does the system of linear equations $x+y+z=2$, $2x+y-z=3$, $3x+2y+Kz=4$ have a unique solution?
en.explanation: A unique solution needs a non-zero coefficient determinant: $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&1\\2&1&-1\\3&2&K\end{vmatrix}=(K+2)-(2K+3)+(4-3)=-K$. So the solution is unique for every $K\ne0$.
notes: At $K=0$ the determinant vanishes (and the system is then inconsistent).
$K=1$ works, but so does every other $K\ne0$.
$K=-1$ works, but so does every other $K\ne0$.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: $AX=B$ has a unique solution exactly when $|A|\ne0$.

en.q: Evaluate the integral $I=\int_0^1x^{\frac12}(1-x)^{\frac32}\,dx$ in terms of Gamma functions.
en.explanation: $\int_0^1x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1}dx=B(m,n)=\frac{\Gamma(m)\Gamma(n)}{\Gamma(m+n)}$. Here $m-1=\frac12$, $n-1=\frac32$, so $m=\frac32$, $n=\frac52$, $m+n=4$: $I=\frac{\Gamma(3/2)\Gamma(5/2)}{\Gamma(4)}=\frac{\pi}{16}$.
notes: Adds 1 to only one of the powers.
Uses the powers themselves, not the powers plus 1.
Adds 2 to the second power; and $\frac32+\frac72=5$, so it would need $\Gamma(5)$.
path: 7.4 Beta and Gamma functions; Wallis' formula
facts: $\int_0^1x^{m-1}(1-x)^{n-1}dx=\frac{\Gamma(m)\Gamma(n)}{\Gamma(m+n)}$: add 1 to each power.

en.q: Find the coefficient of $a_n$ for Fourier series for the square $2\pi$-periodic wave defined on the interval $[-\pi,\pi]$, where $f(x)=\begin{cases}0, & -\pi\le x<0\\1, & 0<x\le\pi\end{cases}$
en.explanation: $a_n=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\cos nx\,dx=\frac1\pi\int_0^\pi\cos nx\,dx=\frac{1}{n\pi}\left[\sin nx\right]_0^\pi=0$ for $n\ge1$.
facts: Here $f(x)-\frac12$ is odd, so only $a_0$ and the sine terms survive.

en.q: Given the initial value problem $\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$, $y(0)=1$ and step size $h=0.1$, find the approximate value of $y(0.1)$ using one step of Euler’s Modified Method.
facts: Modified Euler: $y_1=y_0+\frac h2\left[f(x_0,y_0)+f(x_1,y_0+hf(x_0,y_0))\right]$.

en.q: What is the radius of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{n!}$
en.explanation: $R=\lim\left|\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\right|=\lim\frac{(n+1)!}{n!}=\lim(n+1)=\infty$. The series is $e^z$, convergent for every $z$.
facts: $R=\lim\left|\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\right|$ when this limit exists.

en.q: The rank of the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&0&2\\1&0&3&1\\1&-1&-3&1\\4&-2&0&4\end{bmatrix}$ is equal to ________.
en.explanation: $R_4=2R_1$ and $R_3=R_1-R_2$, so only $R_1$ and $R_2$ are independent (they are not proportional). Rank $=2$.
path: 2.4 Rank and systems of linear equations
facts: Rank $=$ number of linearly independent rows; spot multiples and sums first.

en.q: If $A$ is a $2\times2$ non-singular square matrix, then adj (adj $A$) is
en.explanation: $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|^{n-2}A$. For $n=2$ this is $|A|^0A=A$. (Directly: adj of $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$ swaps $a,d$ and negates $b,c$; doing it twice gives $A$ back.)
facts: $\operatorname{adj}(\operatorname{adj}A)=|A|^{n-2}A$ and $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{n-1}$.

en.q: Given the initial value problem $\frac{dy}{dx}=x+y$, $y(0)=1$, Using the Taylor Series method of order 2 with step size $h=0.1$, calculate the approximate value of $y(0.1)$.
facts: Taylor method of order 2: $y_1=y_0+hy_0'+\frac{h^2}{2}y_0''$.

en.q: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0&0\\1&3&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}-3&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $C=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Then the minimal polynomial of $\begin{pmatrix}A&O&O\\O&B&O\\O&O&C\end{pmatrix}$ is
en.explanation: The minimal polynomial of a block-diagonal matrix is the lcm of those of the blocks. $A-3I\ne O$ but $(A-3I)^2=O$: $m_A=(x-3)^2$. $B=-3I$: $m_B=x+3$. $C\ne O$, $C^2=O$: $m_C=x^2$. So the answer is $x^2(x+3)(x-3)^2$.
notes: Each block's power is too low for A and C.
This is not minimal: $(x+3)$ suffices for $B=-3I$.
That is the characteristic polynomial, not the minimal one.
facts: Minimal polynomial of a block-diagonal matrix $=$ lcm of the blocks' minimal polynomials.

en.q: If $-1, 1, 3$ are different eigenvalues of a given quadratic form, then its canonical form will be:
en.explanation: An orthogonal change of variables reduces a quadratic form to $\lambda_1y_1^2+\lambda_2y_2^2+\lambda_3y_3^2$, with the eigenvalues as coefficients: $-y_1^2+y_2^2+3y_3^2$.
notes: Coefficients are the squares of the eigenvalues.
facts: Canonical form of a quadratic form: $\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$, the $\lambda_i$ being its eigenvalues.

en.q: A periodic function $f(t)$, with period $2\pi$, is represented as its Fourier series $f(t)=a_0+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n\cos nt+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n\sin nt$. If $f(t)=\begin{cases}A\sin t, & 0\le t\le\pi\\0, & \pi<t<2\pi\end{cases}$, the Fourier series coefficient $a_1$ of $f(t)$ is
en.explanation: $a_1=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}f(t)\cos t\,dt=\frac A\pi\int_0^\pi\sin t\cos t\,dt=\frac{A}{2\pi}\left[\sin^2t\right]_0^\pi=0$.
facts: $\int_0^\pi\sin t\cos t\,dt=0$; for the half-wave rectified sine, $a_0=\frac A\pi$, $b_1=\frac A2$, $a_1=0$.

en.q: In the Fourier series expansion of a function $f(x)$ over a general interval of length $4K$, say $[-2K, 2K]$, which term correctly represents the argument of the trigonometric terms (i.e., cos and sin)?
en.explanation: On $[-L,L]$ the terms are $\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}$ and $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$. Here $L=2K$, so the argument is $\frac{n\pi x}{2K}$.
notes: Uses the whole length $4K$ instead of the half-length.
facts: Fourier series on $[-L,L]$ (period $2L$) uses $\cos\frac{n\pi x}{L}$, $\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$.

en.q: Let the function $f(x)$, $x\in\left[-\frac12,\frac12\right]$ given by $f(x)=x-[x]-\frac12$ when $x$ is not an integer and $f(x)=0$ otherwise. Then:
options: f(x) is even function with period 1
f(x) is odd function with period 1
f(x) is even function with period 2
f(x) is odd function with period 2
en.explanation: The formula makes sense for every real $x$, so the period refers to that extension. $x-[x]$ is the fractional part, which has period 1, so $f$ has period 1. For non-integer $x$, $[-x]=-[x]-1$, so $f(-x)=-x+[x]+1-\frac12=-f(x)$; at integers $f=0$. So $f$ is odd with period 1.
notes: Not even, and the least period is 1.
Odd, but the least period is 1.
facts: $x-[x]$ (fractional part) has period 1; $x-[x]-\frac12$ is the odd sawtooth wave.

en.q: The radius of convergence of the power series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{z^{n!}}{n}$ is ________.
en.explanation: The coefficient of $z^k$ is $\frac1n$ when $k=n!$ and 0 otherwise. Cauchy–Hadamard: $\frac1R=\limsup|c_k|^{1/k}=\lim\left(\frac1n\right)^{1/n!}=1$, so $R=1$. (For $|z|<1$ the terms are at most $|z|^n$; for $|z|>1$ they do not tend to 0.)
notes: The radius is a number, not depending on $n$.
facts: Cauchy–Hadamard: $\frac1R=\limsup|c_k|^{1/k}$; it handles series with gaps.

en.q: In practical harmonic analysis, which algorithm is used for calculating the frequency of a discrete signal?
en.explanation: Practical harmonic analysis finds the Fourier coefficients of tabulated (discrete) data. The Fast Fourier Transform computes the discrete Fourier transform in $O(N\log N)$ steps and gives the frequency content.
notes: A transform for continuous functions and ODEs, not an algorithm for discrete data.
facts: Discrete signal to frequencies: discrete Fourier transform, computed by the FFT.

en.q: Which of the following groups is Abelian under the usual operation
en.explanation: Integer addition is commutative and $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is a group, so it is Abelian. Matrix multiplication in $GL(2,\mathbb{R})$ is not commutative, $(\mathbb{Z},\times)$ is not a group (2 has no inverse), and $S_3$ is the smallest non-Abelian group.
notes: Not a group: 2 has no multiplicative inverse in $\mathbb{Z}$.
facts: $S_3$ (order 6) is the smallest non-Abelian group.

en.q: Find the normal form of the bilinear transformation $w=\frac{3iz+1}{z+i}$.
en.explanation: Fixed points: $z(z+i)=3iz+1\Rightarrow z^2-2iz-1=0\Rightarrow(z-i)^2=0$. There is one (double) fixed point $z=i$, so the map is parabolic, with normal form $\frac{1}{w-i}=\frac{1}{z-i}+k$ (here $k=\frac{2c}{a+d}=\frac{2}{4i}=-\frac i2$).
notes: A bilinear map's normal form has no squares.
A bilinear map's normal form has no squares.
path: 10.11 Important results and exam tips: complex numbers
facts: One fixed point $\alpha$ (parabolic): $\frac{1}{w-\alpha}=\frac{1}{z-\alpha}+k$; two fixed points $\alpha,\beta$: $\frac{w-\alpha}{w-\beta}=k\frac{z-\alpha}{z-\beta}$.

en.q: For the function $f(x)=x^2$, $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, if its Fourier series expansion is $f(x)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx)$, then the values of respective Fourier coefficients $a_0$, $a_n$ and $b_n$ are …
en.explanation: $x^2$ is even, so $b_n=0$. $a_0=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}x^2dx=\frac{2\pi^2}{3}$. $a_n=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos nx\,dx=\frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}$ (integrate by parts twice).
facts: $x^2=\frac{\pi^2}{3}+4\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx$ on $[-\pi,\pi]$.

en.q: In metric space, every convergent sequence is:
en.explanation: If $x_n\to x$, then $d(x_m,x_n)\le d(x_m,x)+d(x,x_n)<\varepsilon$ for large $m,n$: the sequence is Cauchy. All but finitely many terms lie in the ball $B(x,1)$, so it is bounded.

en.q: Let $(\mathbb{R}, d)$ be discrete metric space. Then the diameter of the set $S=[-1,1]\cup\left\{\frac32\right\}$ is ______.
en.explanation: In the discrete metric $d(x,y)=1$ whenever $x\ne y$. $S$ has more than one point, so $\operatorname{diam}S=\sup d(x,y)=1$.
notes: That is the diameter in the usual metric.
That is the diameter of $[-1,1]$ in the usual metric.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: In the discrete metric every set with at least two points has diameter 1.

en.q: Let $A$ be a non empty set and $S$ be the set of all functions from $A$ to itself. For $f, g\in S$, define $(f*g)(x)=f(g(x))$ for all $x\in A$. Then which of the following statements is true?
options: $*$ is not a binary operation on $S$
$(S,*)$ is a semigroup but not a group
en.explanation: The composite of two maps $A\to A$ is a map $A\to A$, and composition is associative, so $(S,*)$ is a semigroup (with identity $I_A$). When $A$ has at least two elements, a constant map is not one-one, so it has no inverse: not a group. (If $A$ has only one element, $S=\{I_A\}$ is the trivial group; the question tacitly excludes this case.)
notes: Composition of two maps $A\to A$ is again in $S$.
The identity map $I_A$ is the identity element.
facts: All maps $A\to A$ under composition form a monoid; only the bijections form a group.

en.q: Let $X=\mathbb{R}^2$ be the Euclidean metric space, $B_1$ be the collection of all circular regions in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $B_2$ be the collection of all rectangular regions in $\mathbb{R}^2$. If $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ are the topologies generated by $B_1$ and $B_2$ respectively, then which of the following is true?
en.explanation: Every open disc contains an open rectangle around each of its points, and every open rectangle contains an open disc around each of its points. So each basis generates the other's open sets: both give the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^2$, $\tau_1=\tau_2$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Open discs and open rectangles are bases for the same (usual) topology on $\mathbb{R}^2$.

en.q: Let $X=\{a, b, c\}$ and $\tau_1$, $\tau_2$, $\tau_3$, and $\tau_4$ are collection of subsets of $X$. Then which of the following is not a topology for $X$?
en.explanation: A topology must be closed under unions. In $\tau_3$, $\{a\}\cup\{b\}=\{a,b\}\notin\tau_3$. The other three are closed under unions and finite intersections.

en.q: The residue of $\frac{z^2}{(z-a)(z-b)(z-c)}$ at $z=\infty$ is:
en.explanation: For large $|z|$, $f(z)=\frac1z\left(1-\frac az\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac bz\right)^{-1}\left(1-\frac cz\right)^{-1}=\frac1z+\dots$. The residue at $\infty$ is minus the coefficient of $\frac1z$: $-1$.
notes: Sign: the residue at infinity is minus the $1/z$ coefficient.

en.q: Which of the following is a metric space?
en.explanation: $|x-y|$ is the usual metric on $\mathbb{R}$: non-negative, zero only when $x=y$, symmetric, and it satisfies the triangle inequality. The others fail: $|x|+|y|$ gives $d(1,1)=2$, $|x^2-y^2|$ gives $d(1,-1)=0$, and $x^2-y^2$ can be negative.

en.q: Find the collection which is not a basis for any topology on $X=\{a, b, c\}$.
en.explanation: A basis must cover $X$, and whenever $x\in B\cap B'$ (both in the collection) some member $B''$ satisfies $x\in B''\subseteq B\cap B'$. In $B_2$, $\{a,b\}\cap\{b,c\}=\{b\}$ contains no member of $B_2$. The other three collections pass both tests.
notes: A basis: its members are disjoint and cover $X$.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Basis test: cover $X$, and every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection.

en.q: Evaluate the integral using the Cauchy Residue Theorem: $\int_{|z|=3}\frac{z^2+1}{(z-1)^2(z+2)}\,dz$
en.explanation: Both poles, $z=1$ (double) and $z=-2$, lie inside $|z|=3$. Res at $-2$: $\frac{4+1}{9}=\frac59$. Res at $1$: $\frac{d}{dz}\frac{z^2+1}{z+2}$ at $z=1$ $=\frac{2z(z+2)-(z^2+1)}{(z+2)^2}=\frac{6-2}{9}=\frac49$. Sum $=1$, so the integral is $2\pi i$.
path: 10.11 Important results and exam tips: complex numbers
facts: Shortcut: if all poles are inside, the integral is $2\pi i\times$ (coefficient of $1/z$ at $\infty$); here $f\sim\frac1z$, giving $2\pi i$.

en.q: Let $(\mathbb{R}, d)$ be usual metric space. Which of the following subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is not compact ?
en.explanation: Heine–Borel: in $\mathbb{R}$, compact means closed and bounded. $\{x:\sin x=0\}=\{n\pi:n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is unbounded, so it is not compact. $\{-1,1\}$ is finite, $[0,\pi]$ is closed and bounded, and $\left\{\frac1n\right\}\cup\{0\}$ contains its only limit point 0.
notes: Closed (contains its limit point 0) and bounded.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: Heine–Borel: a subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is compact iff it is closed and bounded.

en.q: Which of the following is true?
options: A subset E of a metric space X is closed if each point of E is a limit point of E
A closed subset of a metric space is compact
A subset E of a metric space X is open if it contains all its interior points
A compact subset of a metric space is closed
en.explanation: A compact subset $K$ of a metric space is closed: for $p\notin K$, the open sets $\{x:d(x,p)>\frac1n\}$ cover $K$, and a finite subcover leaves a ball around $p$ that misses $K$. (a) reverses the definition (closed means every limit point of E lies in E), (b) fails for $[0,\infty)$ in $\mathbb{R}$, and (c) holds for every set (open needs every point of E to be interior).
notes: Reversed: closed means every limit point of E lies in E.
Every set contains its interior points; open means every point is interior.
path: 5.3 Order properties, bounds and point-set topology of R
facts: In a metric space: compact ⟹ closed and bounded (the converse needs $\mathbb{R}^n$).

en.q: A Mobius transformation $T(z)=\frac{az+b}{cz+d}$, $ad-bc\ne0$ is said to be hyperbolic if:
options: It has exactly one fixed point of multiplicity two.
It has two distinct fixed points and is conjugate to a pure dilation $z\mapsto\lambda z$ with $\lambda>0$, $\lambda\ne1$
It has no fixed points in the extended complex plane
It has two distinct fixed points and is conjugate to a rotation $z\mapsto e^{i\theta}z$
en.explanation: A non-identity Möbius map has one or two fixed points. One fixed point: parabolic. Two fixed points: it is conjugate to $z\mapsto\lambda z$, and it is elliptic if $|\lambda|=1$ (rotation), hyperbolic if $\lambda>0$, $\lambda\ne1$ (pure dilation), loxodromic otherwise.
notes: Every Möbius map has a fixed point in $\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$.
path: 10.11 Important results and exam tips: complex numbers
facts: Möbius types: parabolic (one fixed point), elliptic (rotation), hyperbolic (real dilation $\lambda>0$), loxodromic (otherwise).

en.q: What is the purpose of stochastic calculus for finance in continuous-time models?
options: To eliminate all risk from financial portfolios
To determine the exact value of an asset using deterministic models
To provide the complex financial instruments and risk management
To predict future stock prices with perfect accuracy
en.explanation: Stochastic (Itô) calculus models asset prices as random processes in continuous time (Brownian motion). It is used to price complex financial instruments such as options (Black–Scholes) and to manage risk by hedging. It does not remove all risk, is not deterministic, and cannot predict prices exactly.
notes: Risk can be hedged, not eliminated.
The models are random (stochastic), not deterministic.
Prices are modelled as random; exact prediction is impossible.
facts: Stochastic calculus in finance: pricing derivatives and managing risk with random-process models.

en.q: Let $X=\{a, b, c, d\}$ and consider the collection $B=\{\{a\},\{b,c\},\{b,d\}\}$. Which of the following statements is TRUE
options: $B$ is a basis for a topology on $X$, but the set $\{b\}$ does not belong to this topology
$B$ is NOT a basis for any topology on $X$ because the intersection $\{b,c\}\cap\{b,d\}=\{b\}$ cannot be expressed as a union of elements from $B$
$B$ is a basis for a topology on $X$, and the set $\{b\}$ belongs to this topology
$B$ is NOT a basis for any topology on $X$ because it doesn't cover $X$
en.explanation: $B$ covers $X$. But $b\in\{b,c\}\cap\{b,d\}=\{b\}$, and no member of $B$ that contains $b$ lies inside $\{b\}$. So the intersection condition fails and $B$ is not a basis.

facts: A cover is a basis only if every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection.

en.q: Which of the following is a false statement?
options: A function $W=f(z)$ is a conformal mapping if it is Analytic and $\frac{d(f(z))}{dz}\ne0$ everywhere in its domain.
The inverse of a conformal mapping is also conformal.
A function $W=f(z)$ is a conformal mapping if it is Analytic and $\frac{d(f(z))}{dz}=0$ everywhere in its domain.
The composition of two conformal mappings is also a conformal mapping.
en.explanation: An analytic map preserves angles where $f'(z)\ne0$. If $f'(z)=0$ everywhere on a domain, $f$ is constant and squashes the domain to a point, so it is not conformal. The other three statements are standard facts.
notes: True: the standard condition for conformality.
True: the chain rule gives a non-zero derivative.
facts: Analytic with $f'(z)\ne0$ ⟹ conformal; $f'\equiv0$ ⟹ $f$ constant.

en.q: The $2\times2$ Haar matrix which is associated with Haar wavelet is:
en.explanation: The Haar transform of a pair $(x_1,x_2)$ gives their sum (average) and their difference (detail): $\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$, up to the factor $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Its rows are the scaling function $(1,1)$ and the Haar wavelet $(1,-1)$.

facts: $H_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{bmatrix}$: sums and differences of neighbouring values.
